metadata.title: Embodied Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Manipulation Planning With Embodied World Model
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper proposes a novel planning framework called Embodied Tree of Thoughts (EToT) that leverages a physics-based interactive digital twin as an embodied world model for robot manipulation planning. EToT ensures that generated plans adhere to rigid-body dynamics and collision constraints, and it consistently outperforms baselines in predicting physical dynamics and adapting to potential failures.

sections.heading: Planning With Embodied World Model
sections.text: Wenjiang Xu , Mingkang Zhang, Cindy Wang, Rui Fang, Lusong Li, Jing Xu , Member, IEEE , Jiayuan Gu , Zecui Zeng , and Rui Chen , Member, IEEE Abstract —World models have emerged as a pivotal component in robot manipulation planning, enabling agents to predict future environmental states and reason about the consequences of actions before execution. While video-generation models are increasingly adopted, they often lack rigorous physical grounding, leading to hallucinations and a failure to maintain consistency in long-horizon physical constraints. To address these limitations, we propose Em- bodied Tree of Thoughts (EToT), a novel Real2Sim2Real planning framework that leverages a physics-based interactive digital twin as an embodied world model. EToT formulates manipulation plan- ning as a tree search expanded through two synergistic mecha- nisms: (1) Priori Branching, which generates diverse candidate execution paths based on semantic and spatial analysis; and (2) Reflective Branching, which utilizes VLMs to diagnose execution failures within the simulator and iteratively refine the planning tree with corrective actions. By grounding high-level reasoning in a physics simulator, our framework ensures that generated plans adhere to rigid-body dynamics and collision constraints. We validate EToT on a suite of short- and long-horizon manipulation tasks, where it consistently outperforms baselines by effectively predicting physical dynamics and adapting to potential failures. Index Terms —Failure detection and recovery, manipulation planning, robot safety, task and motion planning. I. However, these approaches primarily operate on static scene representations and lack the physical intuition required to predict the dynamic evolution of the environment under long-horizon action sequences. To address this limitation, world models that predict future states conditioned on robot actions have attracted increasing attention. A line of recent work adopts video generation models as forward predictors of future scenes for grounded planning [4] . While effective for short-term prediction, such pixel-space mod- els lack explicit physical grounding and struggle to capture the cumulative effects of contact-rich interactions, often producing physically inconsistent “hallucinations” over long horizons [5] . sections.text: ETHODOLOGY We propose the Embodied Tree of Thoughts (EToT) frame- work (Fig. 2 ), which extends the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by coupling them with a physics-based embodied world model and a planning-tree search mechanism. The proposed methodology is organized around the following core questions: (1) How are robot action skills formally defined? (Section III-A ) (2) How is a high-fidelity and interactive digital twin constructed? (Section III-B ) (3) How is a world-model-grounded planning tree constructed and searched? (Section III-C ) A. Action Skills Set In this work, we focus on the task planning aspect of robotic manipulation. To standardize the planning process and facilitate the logical structuring of action sequences by the VLM, we model robot skills as a set of discrete semantic action primitives. Specifically, we define the following five action skills: [PICK UP, obj] , [PUT ON, surface] , [PUT INTO, con- tainer] , [OPEN, obj] , and [CLOSE, obj] . However, for objects that afford multiple distinct grasping ori- entations and for which identifying a feasible pose is nontrivial, we provide additional pose-specific configurations, denoted as [PICK UP, obj] (POSE) , to enable disambiguation among alternative grasp strategies. B. Embodied World Model Construction We construct an embodied world model using an efficient scene reconstruction pipeline that, in most cases, requires only a single RGB-D observation. Given an input RGB-D frame, we first extract object masks from the RGB image [18] and use SAM-3D [7] to generate initial textured object meshes. However, since the scales of meshes from SAM-3D may be incorrect, we jointly estimate the object poses and scales (Fig. 3 ): we first estimate object pose with FoundationPose [19] using the generated mesh, compare the mesh mask projected into the RGB image with the observed mask, project both onto the three axes of the mesh local coordinate frame, and then adjust the mesh scale along each axis using the corresponding extent ratios. Object density is estimated by the VLM [2] , while friction and other physical parameters use simulator de- faults. Finally, the reconstructed meshes are imported into the OmniGibson [8] physics simulator to generate an aligned and interactive digital twin of the physical scene. For scenes containing articulated objects, an additional RGB- D frame captured with the object in an alternative kinematic state (e.g., open versus closed) is required. In the current system, this state change is performed with manual assistance before capturing the additional observation. These multi-state observa- tions are then processed using DexSim2Real 2 [20] to recover the articulated structure. C. Planning Tree Construction and Searching As illustrated in Fig. 2 , we construct a world-model–grounded planning tree to support manipulation planning. The planning process consists of two key modules: Priori Branching and Re- flective Branching. Priori Branching is responsible for generat- ing the initial planning tree; however, the resulting branches may be invalid or unsafe due to incomplete physical reasoning. To address these issues, Reflective Branching analyzes simulated execution outcomes, identifies failure causes, and dynamically generates revised branches during the tree search process. The overall planning procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1 . 1) Priori Branching: In the initial stage, the VLM analyzes the scene and task instruction to construct a preliminary plan- ning tree grounded in object instances and candidate interaction modes. Scene Parsing and Task Understanding: The VLM takes as input an RGB image of the scene together with the task in- struction. It extracts object-level information and infers relevant spatial relationships, including relational predicates (e.g., “the pen is on the drawer”) and articulation states (e.g., “the drawer is closed”). Candidate Branches Generation: Based on the parsed scene representation, the VLM generates multiple candidate planning branches, each corresponding to a complete action sequence from the root to a leaf. The model is encouraged to explicitly branch at decision points where multiple feasible action choices exist. CombinedwithReflectiveBranchinganddynamicplanrevision, this strategy enables efficient discovery of feasible task plans while preserving both robustness and reasoning depth. During search, each node is evaluated sequentially along a branch: if the action is judged feasible by the VLM, the search proceeds to its children; otherwise, it enters the Reflective Branching stage. If a successful leaf node is reached, extractPath ( N ) returns the single feasible root-to-leaf plan ending at N . In contrast, when a node fails, extractPaths ( N ) returns all affected root-to-leaf paths passing through the failed node and therefore requiring revision. During branch merging, N merged denotes the nodes in the new branch that overlap with the existing tree, while n new denotes the first newly inserted non-overlapping node pushed into the search queue. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , Reflective Branching consists of the following two procedures: r Failure Detection: Successful execution requires not only achieving the task objective but also avoiding unintended disturbances or damage to surrounding objects. An ex- ecution is classified as unsafe if it induces environmental changes that cannot be easily recovered using the available action skills, such as a tennis ball rolling off the table or a pen falling beyond the robot’s reachable workspace. r Tree Correction and Expansion: Upon detecting execution failures or undesirable side effects, the VLM diagnoses the cause and proposes a corrective strategy. In this work, we consider two categories: (i) Collision-induced distur- bances: if the planned motion would collide with nearby objects and alter their states, the affected objects are first relocated to safe positions before reattempting the original action. (ii) Ordering-related conflicts: some failures arise from improper action ordering. For example, in Task 6 (Section IV-B ), inserting the apple into the holder before relocating the holder prevents subsequent grasping. In such cases, the branch is revised by reordering the relevant actions. D. Construction of Closed-Loop System We further develop a closed-loop execution framework with real-robot feedback. After each action, the VLM evaluates the execution outcome using real camera observations. If a failure is detected, the system reconstructs the current scene as a new initialstateandreplansfromitundertheoriginaltaskinstruction. This enables continuous feedback-driven correction during real- world execution. IV. E XPERIMENTS In this section, we first describe the experimental setup (Section IV-A ) and task design (Section IV-B ). We then re- port the main experimental results (Section IV-C ) and ablation studies (Section IV-D ), followed by analyses of failure modes, reconstruction accuracy, VLM module accuracy, and compu- tational efficiency (Section IV-E ), and parallel acceleration (Section IV-F ). A. Experimental Setup Hardware: As illustrated in Fig. 4 , all experiments are con- ducted using an xArm6 6DoF robot manipulator with a parallel- jaw gripper and an Azure Kinect RGB-D camera. Baselines: We compare our method against three baselines.

Upon detecting a failure, an oracle-style reflection step is invoked, in which a valid recovery plan is manually specified using the available action primitives whenever such a plan exists. As these keypoint-based baselines use a different planning format, we enhance them by providing ground-truth keypoints and manually aligning their generated plans to our action-skill setting. Metrics: We evaluate each method by task success rate , defined as the proportion of trials that achieve the specified goal without causing harmful changes to the environment. Implementation Details: All baselines and our proposed method are implemented using GPT-4o [2] as the underlying vision language model. The camera is mounted at a fixed oblique viewing angle. For each task, all experiments are repeated for 30 independent trials. B. Task Design We design a suite of seven manipulation tasks to systemati- cally evaluate four fundamental capabilities of robotic planning: (a) awareness of object manipulability, (b) understanding of three-dimensional spatial relationships, (c) prediction of physi- cal dynamics, and (d) robustness to external disturbances with automatic recovery. Tasks with three or fewer action steps are categorized as short-horizon tasks (Tasks 1–4), whereas those with more than three actions are classified as long-horizon tasks (Tasks 5–7). We also include a disturbance-aware task with human-induced interference during execution. Fig. 5 provides an overview of all tasks. Besides the objects shown in each task, Fig. 5 (right) includes an additional pen instance and an additional drawer instance. In the corresponding tasks, the object is randomly selected from all instances of that category to improve exper- imental generalization. Task 1. Open the door of the microwave oven: ( b, c ) Directly opening the door would cause the tennis ball on the desk to fall; the ball must therefore be relocated prior to door actuation. Task 2. C. Experimental Results and Discussion Table I summarizes the success rates of our method in compar- ison with all baselines across the seven tasks. Our approach con- sistently outperforms the baselines on every task and achieves the highest overall average success rate of 80.42% . ReKep generates constraint-based plans grounded in VLM- predicted keypoints; however, its limited fine-grained three- dimensional spatial reasoning and physical dynamics prediction lead to poor performance across most tasks, resulting in the lowest overall success rate. ReKep w/ CoT augments ReKep with additional chain-of-thought reasoning, yielding notice- able improvements on Tasks 1 and 4. In these tasks, it more often identifies obstructing objects and plans their removal appropriately. Nevertheless, its performance gains on the re- maining tasks remain limited. Reflect ∗ further incorporates reflective planning and demon- strates clear improvements on Task 3, where an initial failed horizontal grasp can be corrected by a subsequent top-down attempt. It also performs comparably to our method on the Disturbance Task by adapting its plan after execution failures. However, even with oracle-level reflective reasoning, Reflect provides no benefit in tasks involving irreversible failures (e.g., Task 6, where the apple cannot be recovered once it falls into the holder). In contrast, our method leverages a physics-based world model to identify potential risks prior to execution, and proactively generate safer plans to avoid such failures. On long-horizon tasks, all three baselines exhibit limited performance, with none exceeding a 50% success rate, due to the increased complexity of spatial constraints and extended branching factors. By contrast, our method exploits the predic- tive capability of the physics world model and performs a more comprehensive VLM-guided tree search, maintaining high suc- cess rates on Tasks 5–7 (21/30, 23/30, and 18/30, respectively). D. Ablation Table II summarizes the ablation results for Priori Branching, Reflective Branching, real-world Replanning, and replacing the physics simulator with a VGM [23] . For VGM-based planning, each action starts from the real camera image, and the VGM pre- dicts the execution video conditioned on the action instruction. Removing either Priori Branching or Reflective Branching causes substantial performance degradation. Without Priori Branching, the VLM produces a single-branch search tree and often commits to incorrect high-level decisions in multi-path tasks

Scene Analysis, Density Estimation, and Priori Branching achieve perfect accuracy, where density estimation is judged by estimate reasonableness and sim-real alignment of relevant object states after action execution, while Reflective Branching and VLM Judge reach 98.75% and 96.74%. Reflective Branch- ing errors occur on Task 7, and VLM Judge errors on Tasks 2 and 5; the judge also shows 1.20% false positives and 0% false negatives, indicating strong reliability. From the efficiency perspective, Fig. 8 shows that the VLM- related overhead is dominated by the Judge module, which consumes the largest share of runtime and tokens because it is repeatedly invoked during execution verification. Neverthe- less, the overall planning overhead remains comparable to real execution time and is not prohibitive. Averaged over all tasks, ReKep, ReKep w/ CoT, and Reflect ∗ require 1325.57, 2742.34, and 2742.34 VLM tokens and 80.21, 87.82, and 114.79 s, respectively, while EToT uses 13341.63 tokens and 153.00 s, but achieves substantially higher success rates and more reliable safety. This limited extra cost brings clear gains in both task success rate and execution safety. F. Parallel Acceleration Tree-based planning becomes increasingly expensive as the search depth and branching factor grow. To improve efficiency, we adopt a multi-world parallelism strategy, where newly generated child nodes are evaluated in parallel from their parent terminal states. This design works naturally with BFS: since the depth of a leaf directly corresponds to the number of high-level actions in the candidate plan, BFS explores the tree layer by layer and favors shorter feasible solutions, while same-parent child nodes can be rolled out concurrently without violating causal structure. In practice, this reduces the simulation time of Task 5 from 55 s to 26 s, showing that parallel execution substantially improves the practicality of the method. V. C ONCLUSION This work presents Embodied Tree of Thoughts (EToT), a deliberative manipulation planning framework that integrates tree-structured search with a physics-based embodied world model. By jointly leveraging Priori Branching and Reflective Branching , EToT enhances physical reasoning, anticipates po- tential execution failures prior to real-world deployment, and generates robust and safe manipulation plans. Extensive experi- mental results demonstrate that EToT consistently outperforms existing approaches, with particularly significant advantages on complex long-horizon tasks where sequential dependencies and physical constraints are critical. Additional analyses further demonstrate the accuracy and practicality of its reconstruction and VLM reasoning modules. At present, the proposed framework is effective for tabletop manipulation
